content: The following interventions and studies focus on strategies to reduce unnecessary cesarean sections, with detailed methodologies and outcomes: 1. Mandatory Second Opinion (Althabe et al., 2004): A mandatory second opinion was required before performing a cesarean section. The second opinion had to be provided by a physician with equal or higher clinical qualifications than the attending physician, working in the same hospital, and selected by the obstetrics department. These physicians agreed to follow evidence-based clinical guidelines, which were presented as decision flowcharts for six primary indications for cesarean sections. 2. Peer Review and Mandatory Second Opinion (Liang et al., 2004): This intervention included pre-cesarean consultations and post-cesarean surveillance. Two physicians were appointed as consultants for pre-cesarean surveillance, and a second opinion was mandatory for all cesarean sections. Additionally, all cesarean cases were presented at weekly meetings by the chief resident. 3. Audit and Feedback Using the Robson Classification (Scarella et al., 2011): An initial audit and feedback were provided to maternity and midwifery staff, focusing on the main contributors to the overall cesarean section rate using the Robson classification. Examples of cesarean sections performed without clinical justification were discussed, emphasizing the need to safely reduce cesarean rates in specific groups. Monthly audits followed, with feedback provided via individual letters to staff. Quarterly meetings were held to present changes in cesarean rates and five-minute Apgar scores below seven, with data ranked by duty-day shifts. Reports were also sent to all maternity staff. 4. Audit and Feedback Plus Financial Incentive (Mohammadi, Källestål, & Essén, 2012): A clinical audit reviewed random samples of cesarean section cases to assess indications. Financial incentives were provided to practitioners who met the criteria for appropriate cesarean use. 5. Evidence-Based Guidelines Plus Audit and Feedback (Chaillet et al., 2015): Evidence-based clinical practice guidelines were implemented through on-site training, facilitation by local opinion leaders, and supervision. Audits of cesarean indications were conducted, and feedback was provided to health professionals. 6. Audit and Feedback Plus 24-Hour In-House Coverage (Poma, 1998): Labor management and cesarean delivery guidelines were implemented, with reviews of all cesarean deliveries that did not meet the guidelines. Confidential individual feedback was provided. A 24-hour in-house coverage system was established, with an attending physician present to manage labor and complications. The goal was to achieve an annual cesarean delivery rate of less than 15%. 7. Audit and Feedback Plus Local Opinion Leader Education (Lomas et al., 1991): This intervention involved agreed criteria for cesarean use in women with previous cesarean sections, medical audits comparing actual practices with these criteria, and departmental meetings every three months for feedback and discussion. Local opinion leaders were identified and trained in evidence-based guidelines and behavior change principles. They hosted educational meetings, maintained formal and informal educational contacts, and supported guideline implementation. 8. Expanded Access to Collaborative 24-Hour Midwifery-Laborist Care Model (Rosenstein et al., 2015): One midwife and one laborist were present in-house 24 hours a day, working collaboratively to manage labor for all private and public patients. 9. Financial Interventions Targeted at Health-Care Professionals (Keeler & Fok, 1996; Lo, 2008): Physician fees for vaginal and cesarean deliveries were equalized to reduce financial incentives for cesarean sections. In Taiwan, the fee for vaginal birth after cesarean (VBAC) was raised to match that of cesarean sections in 2003, and the fee for vaginal births was increased to the same level in 2005. These interventions highlight a range of strategies, including mandatory second opinions, peer reviews, audits, feedback, financial incentives, and collaborative care models, aimed at reducing unnecessary cesarean sections while maintaining safe and evidence-based practices.
